title: The Lantern Workshop: Four Signal Puzzles
designRationale: The contract requires four independent-evidence items (C1 equal-group structure, C3 array reading, C2 equation mapping, C4 factor-referent discrimination) with no hints, feedback, or answer exposure until all responses are recorded. The design challenge is to give a nine-year-old who likes hard riddles and questions faulty logic (reina:riddles:harder, reina:riddles:logic) a compelling reason to answer honestly four times in a row without any correctness feedback. The chosen frame is a 'signal workshop': the child is a lantern-keeper who inspects four sealed signal crates and files an honest inspection report for each. Framing the child as an INSPECTOR rather than a quiz-taker makes withheld feedback narratively coherent — inspectors file reports and the results come back later, so silence after each answer feels like the world working, not the interface breaking. It also dignifies 'not sure': an inspector who is unsure marks the crate 'needs another look', which is a legitimate professional act, matching the contract's requirement that not_sure is recorded as missing evidence rather than failure. The riddle-loving evidence is treated strictly as an engagement hypothesis: ITEM-4's same-product trap is presented as 'the trick crate', signaling that careful thinking is expected, without teaching or previewing structure. All stimuli, factor pairs, prompts, option sets, sequencing (ITEM-1→2→3→4), credit rules, exposure identities, and the no-exposure window are preserved exactly as contracted. Visual grouping and color aid parsing but never encode the answer (per the presentation-burden hypothesis). Response modes are large-target tap selection and stepper-style numeric pickers (tap up/down or tap a number tile 1–10), so reading, typing, and pointer precision stay out of the measured construct. One stimulus per screen, no time limit, child may stop at any moment via an always-visible 'close the workshop for today' door.
independentlyChosenPrinciples: Feedback silence must be diegetic: the fiction (inspection reports filed, results pending) explains why the world does not say right/wrong, so the child never experiences withheld feedback as malfunction.
Uncertainty is a first-class professional action: 'Needs another look' is drawn, worded, and animated with the same visual dignity as a numeric answer, so choosing it costs no face.

Every required action must be demonstrable by the screen itself: the first crate's answer slots pulse gently and are labeled with icons plus one short word, so a non-reading child could still discover what to do.
Color and grouping cues may make quantities parseable but must be answer-neutral: all clusters share one accent color; nothing highlights the correct count, row, or option.
Input mechanics must have lower ceremony than the mathematics: number tiles 1–10 in a fixed keypad grid, tap once to fill a slot, tap the slot again to clear — no dragging, no typing, no scrolling.

Commitment must be explicit and reversible until sealed: the child can change any entry freely until pressing the large 'Seal the report' stamp; only sealing records the response, preventing accidental-tap evidence.
Stakes come from role and craft, not from scores: no points, streaks, timers, or right/wrong meters exist anywhere in the evaluation window.
The trap item is honored, not hidden: ITEM-4 is introduced as 'the trick crate' to invite the riddle-solver's care, but no content hint about WHAT the trick is ever appears.
openingPromise: One full-screen line, read aloud by the interface on tap of a speaker icon: 'The signal tower needs its lanterns tonight. Four crates just arrived. You are the Inspector. Check each crate, file your report, and the tower lights at the end.' The promise is concrete (four crates, tower lights), finite (exactly four), and role-granting (you are the Inspector) — an immediately understandable reason to act.
firstThreeSeconds: Second 0–1: a dim workshop interior fades in; a warm lantern glow pools at the center where Crate 1 sits, already open, showing the four bunches of six dots (glowing beads). Second 1–2: the single stimulus sentence appears beneath the crate in large type with a tappable speaker icon that reads it aloud; nothing else competes for attention. Second 2–3: the two answer slots slide up from the bottom — a 'bunches' slot with a small cluster icon and a 'dots in each bunch' slot with a single-bead icon — and both pulse once, while the 1–10 number keypad fades in beside them. The child can act within three seconds without reading a manual: tap a number, it fills the pulsing slot.
firstAction: Tap one number tile (1–10) to fill the first pulsing answer slot ('How many bunches?'). The slot pulses until filled; tapping a tile fills whichever slot is currently highlighted; tapping a filled slot clears it. The visible alternative actions on the same screen are the 'Needs another look' magnifier button (records not_sure) and the speaker icon (reads the sentence aloud, mitigating the reading confound). No other interaction exists on screen one, so the first required action is unambiguous from the finished screen alone.
mission: Serve one night shift as the Signal Workshop Inspector: examine four sealed lantern crates in fixed order (dot-bead crate, tile-panel crate, equation-label crate, and the trick crate), file one honest report per crate — including 'Needs another look' when unsure — and, once all four reports are sealed, raise the signal tower and light it. The mission ends when every crate has a recorded outcome or when the Inspector chooses to close the workshop early.
coreInteraction: Each crate is one screen with exactly one stimulus (contract items 1–4, verbatim in content and constraints). The loop: (1) crate opens and reveals the stimulus; (2) the prompt appears in one short sentence with a read-aloud speaker; (3) the child fills the response fields — numeric slots via a 1–10 tap keypad for ITEM-1 and ITEM-2, a single tap-to-select from four equation labels for ITEM-3, and a same/different toggle plus one numeric slot for ITEM-4 — or taps 'Needs another look'; (4) the child presses the large 'Seal the report' stamp, which commits the response with a wax-stamp animation; (5) a conveyor carries the sealed crate to the shipping shelf and the next crate slides in. No correctness signal of any kind accompanies sealing: every sealed crate gets the identical neutral stamp regardless of the answer. Entries are freely editable before sealing; nothing is recorded until the stamp.
mathAsPower: The mathematics IS the inspection instrument: reading equal-group structure is the only way to fill a crate report, because the report fields are exactly the mathematical quantities (groups, per-group; rows, per-row; matching equation; same-vs-different situation plus referent count). The child affects the world solely by committing mathematical judgments — each sealed report physically moves a crate to the shelf and adds one rung of scaffolding to the signal tower silhouette on the side wall. There is no non-mathematical path to progress: decoration, exploration, and the speaker button change nothing in the world; only sealed mathematical reports advance the shift. Crucially, the power granted is causal, not evaluative: the tower rises because reports were FILED (attempted/committed), not because they were correct, preserving truthful evidence while still letting math be the lever that moves the experience.
responseAffordances: Numeric fields (ITEM-1, ITEM-2, ITEM-4 basket count): a fixed on-screen keypad of ten large tiles (1–10), minimum 72×72 px targets at 1365×768; tap fills the highlighted slot; tap a filled slot to clear; no typing, no keyboard, no drag.

Two-field items highlight one slot at a time with an icon + one-word label (bunches/dots, rows/squares) so field roles are visually distinct; the child can tap either slot to switch highlight, so answer order is never forced.

ITEM-3 equation choice: four large label cards in a 2×2 grid, fixed but randomized-once order stored with the record (position-bias audit); tap selects with a visible border, tap again deselects; only one selectable at a time.

ITEM-4: a two-button toggle ('Same situation' / 'Different situations') with plain-language captions read aloud on the speaker tap, plus one numeric slot for baskets in Statement A; the ambiguous word 'same' is presented exactly per contract wording in the prompt while the buttons carry the fuller captions to reduce, not remove, the documented ambiguity confound (flag preserved regardless).
'Needs another look' magnifier button on every screen, same visual weight as the seal stamp, records not_sure for the whole item (or per field on ITEM-4) and advances normally.
Speaker icon on every text element reads it aloud (pre-recorded, neutral voice) to keep reading fluency out of the measured construct; each read-aloud use is logged as an accommodation, not scored.
'Seal the report' stamp is disabled until every field holds either a value or not_sure, preventing accidental omissions; a gentle wiggle on a disabled tap shows which field is empty.
'Close the workshop' door icon persists top-left; tapping it asks one confirmation ('Done for tonight?') and ends the session, recording unreached items as missing evidence.
stakesAndConsequences: The stakes are craft and completion, not correctness: each sealed report is one lantern crate cleared and one rung of the signal tower built, and the night shift only ends well if the crates are dealt with — by an answer OR by an honest 'Needs another look'. Consequences are real but dignity-preserving: a sealed crate cannot be reopened (the wax stamp is final), so committing an answer matters and the child feels the weight of the decision at the stamp moment, not after. There is no penalty state, no lost progress, and no visible tally of anything except crates handled. Crates marked 'Needs another look' ride the conveyor to a clearly labeled 'second-look shelf' rather than the shipping shelf — a visible, respectful consequence that tells the truth (this one is unresolved) without shaming. Stopping early closes the workshop with the tower partially built and the unfinished crates still waiting under a cloth — a truthful, non-punitive image of missing evidence.
recovery: No response can trap the child. Before sealing: any entry is clearable and changeable indefinitely; there is no time limit and no forced field order. Uncertainty: 'Needs another look' is always one tap away and advances the shift exactly like an answer. Instrument ambiguity: if the child taps the seal with a field empty, the empty field wiggles and nothing is recorded — no error text, no sound sting. Mis-taps: keypad tiles fill only the highlighted slot, and slots are individually clearable, so a stray tap costs one tap to undo. After sealing: the child cannot revise (evidence integrity), but the world never dwells — the next crate arrives immediately, so an uneasy feeling about a sealed report has no lingering screen to fixate on. Wanting to stop: the door is always available, ends the session in two taps, and the closing scene is warm regardless of how many crates were handled ('The workshop rests. The crates will keep.'). If the child stalls silently, nothing escalates: the screen stays calm, the lantern glow breathes slowly, and after 60 seconds the speaker icon pulses once as a wordless reminder that the prompt can be read aloud — a friction mitigation, never a hint about content.
progression: Visible progression is the tower and the shelf: a side-wall silhouette of the signal tower gains one glowing rung per sealed report (four rungs total), and handled crates accumulate physically on the shipping or second-look shelf. Crate order is the contract's fixed sequence (ITEM-1 → ITEM-2 → ITEM-3 → ITEM-4), and the crates are visibly different objects — beads, tile panel, printed labels, and a smaller ornate 'trick crate' with a riddle-knot on its clasp — so each screen feels like new territory rather than repetition, honoring the child's demonstrated dislike of repeated puzzles (reina:riddles:logic). A small chalkboard reads 'Crate 2 of 4' so the finite length is always visible. The trick crate is announced only as trickier ('This one fooled the last inspector'), leveraging the harder-riddles hypothesis to frame the hardest discrimination item as the honored finale without previewing its structure. No difficulty adaptation occurs; item content, order, and boundaries are immutable.
worldReaction: Every commitment gets the same truthful, answer-blind reaction: the wax stamp thunks, the crate lid latches, the conveyor hums it to a shelf, and one tower rung glows. Correct, incorrect, and uncertain responses are visually indistinguishable at the moment of reaction — the only differentiation is destination shelf (shipping for answered, second-look for not_sure), which reflects the child's own declared state, never hidden scoring. Recovered actions (clearing a slot, switching a selection) get a soft chalk-erase wipe so editing feels sanctioned. Empty-field seal attempts get the wiggle-and-wait reaction. Early exit gets the workshop-at-rest scene. Because the fiction says results 'come back from the tower keepers later', the absence of right/wrong reaction reads as world logic, and no reaction ever exposes an answer, models a solution, or hints before the evaluation window closes.
payoff: When the fourth report is sealed (by answer or not_sure), the workshop wall opens onto the night sky and the signal tower lights in a slow, warm sequence — one lamp per handled crate — ending with a wide shot of the lit tower over the valley and a single line: 'Shift complete. Four crates handled. The tower saw your work.' The payoff celebrates completion and honest inspection, never accuracy: it is identical for any mix of answered and not_sure crates, and proportionally scaled (fewer lamps) if the child stopped early, so the reward cannot leak correctness information or pressure the child toward guessing over honesty. Only AFTER this scene, per the contract's post-window allowance, may an optional 'Ask the tower keeper' hint/curiosity affordance be offered for any crate on the second-look shelf — clearly outside the evaluation, separately logged, and never rewriting the sealed evidence.
replayVariation: This artifact's four exposures (EX-EQGROUPS-DOTS-4x6, EX-ARRAY-GRID-3x7, EX-EQUATION-MATCH-5x3, EX-REFERENT-SWAP-2x8) are single-use: replay of this exact session is prohibited because re-seeing the items contaminates independence and the ITEM-3 option set is answer-adjacent exposure. Replay is therefore designed as 'another night shift' with structurally distinct crates drawn from the contract's evidenceRequiredNext list — a no-picture equal-group crate, an unknown-factor crate, a column-orientation array crate, and a disambiguation crate for ITEM-4 'same' responses — each with new factor pairs, new context families, and new exposure IDs, authored under the same boundaries (factors 1–10, products ≤100, no exposure reuse). The workshop shell, inspector role, and interaction grammar persist across nights so no re-learning of the interface is needed, but no stimulus, factor pair, option set, or exposure identity ever recurs. If a replay is requested before new items exist, the workshop offers only the interface-familiar but math-free 'crate-sorting warm-up' (usable as the contract's non-mathematical latency baseline task) rather than reusing evaluation content.
visualDirection: Warm, low-clutter workshop interior: deep indigo shadows, amber lantern light, matte wood textures; one crate, one sentence, one response area per screen with generous whitespace. Countable stimuli use a single saturated accent (lantern-gold beads/squares) on a dark neutral crate interior for maximum figure-ground contrast; clusters are separated by clear dark gaps sized so counting needs no zooming at 1365×768. Color is answer-neutral: all groups, rows, and options share the same accent; nothing color-codes correctness. Text is large (≥28 px stimulus sentence, ≥24 px labels), short, high-contrast cream-on-indigo, one sentence at a time, honoring the low-text-load hypothesis and the small-sample preference for visible color and clear layout — while the 'clear examples' preference is deliberately NOT honored inside the window, since examples are contractually excluded until all items are recorded. Keypad tiles, option cards, and the seal stamp are the largest interactive elements on screen; the not_sure magnifier matches the stamp's size and finish so it never looks like a lesser choice.
motionDirection: Motion is calm and functional: crates slide in over ~600 ms with an ease-out settle; answer slots pulse at a slow 1.2 s breathing rhythm only while empty and highlighted; keypad taps give a 120 ms press-down and the number gliding into the slot; clearing a slot plays a 200 ms chalk-erase wipe. The seal stamp is the ceremonial beat: stamp descends, wax squashes, crate latches (~800 ms total) — deliberately weighty so commitment feels consequential. Conveyor transit between items is ~1.5 s, giving a breath between crates without dead time. Tower rungs light with a soft 400 ms bloom. Nothing moves during reading or deliberation except the slow lantern-glow breathing; no idle animations compete with counting; no motion ever gestures toward a particular number, cell, row, or option. All motion respects reduced-motion settings by degrading to simple fades.
soundDirection: Quiet workshop room tone (fire crackle, distant wind) at low volume, muteable via a persistent icon. Interaction sounds are informational, never evaluative: soft wood tick for keypad taps, paper slide for slot fills, chalk swish for clears, a satisfying single wax-thunk for sealing that is IDENTICAL for every response type so audio cannot leak correctness, and a low conveyor hum between crates. The read-aloud voice is a warm neutral adult voice, plainly paced, triggered only by the speaker icon — never auto-playing over the child's thinking. The finale uses a rising four-note lamp motif, one note per handled crate, tuned to completion count, not accuracy. No error buzzers, no correctness chimes, no music with lyrics, no escalating urgency loops anywhere.
usefulLibraries: Svelte or Preact — small reactive UI for the four single-stimulus screens and slot/keypad state without framework overhead.
GSAP (or Motion One) — the crate slide, stamp squash, conveyor transit, and tower-bloom timelines with reduced-motion fallbacks.
Howler.js — reliable touch-unlocked audio for room tone, interaction ticks, and pre-recorded read-aloud clips with a global mute.
PixiJS (optional) — crisp rendering of the bead clusters and tile array if DOM/SVG counting fidelity proves insufficient at scale; otherwise plain SVG suffices.
idb-keyval (IndexedDB) — durable local event log (responses, latencies, read-aloud uses, seal timestamps, exit events) so evidence survives a dropped connection.
date-fns or native performance.now() — monotonic latency capture for c1–c4 time-to-first-entry and selection-latency keys, immune to wall-clock changes.
anticipatedChildConfusions: ITEM-1: she may count all 24 beads and report the total in one slot; the slot icons (cluster vs. single bead) and one-word labels reduce this, and a total-in-slot pattern (e.g., 24 entered but rejected by 1–10 keypad bounds) is logged as c1_reported_total_instead_of_pair pressure — note the 1–10 keypad structurally prevents entering 24, which itself may confuse a total-seeking child; the slot wiggle on impossible intent is the recovery path.

ITEM-1/ITEM-2: role reversal (which slot is groups vs. per-group, rows vs. per-row) — icons disambiguate visually, but reversals are expected diagnostic outcomes and are recorded per the credit rules, never prevented by the interface.
ITEM-2: she may read columns as rows; the prompt word 'rows' is read-aloudable but never illustrated with a highlight (that would teach); orientation confusion is captured by c3_roles_reversed.

ITEM-3: she may pick 5 x 3 = 15 by recognizing the product after counting all items; the interface cannot prevent this and does not try — the latency key and cross-item consistency checks carry that burden.

ITEM-4: the word 'same' may be read as 'same total'; the toggle captions ('Same situation'/'Different situations') narrow but cannot eliminate this; any 'same' response is flagged ambiguous pending the contracted follow-up probe, never scored as plain error.

Interface: she may expect the stamp to tell her if she was right (riddle-app habits); the opening narration pre-empts this ('reports come back from the tower keepers later'), and identical stamp feedback keeps the expectation from becoming distrust.

She may look for the hint button she liked in prior activities (reina:activity-feedback:small-sample); no hint exists inside the window by contract, and 'Needs another look' plus the post-window 'Ask the tower keeper' are the sanctioned outlets; frustration at missing hints is logged as friction, not ability evidence.
instrumentRisks: Keypad bounds (1–10) silently prevent total-reporting behaviors the contract wants to observe (e.g., entering 24 or 21), potentially masking the reported_total confound rather than measuring it; mitigation: log every out-of-affordance intent signal available (rapid multi-tile taps, repeated slot clearing) and flag the item's confound field.

Slot icons on ITEM-1/ITEM-2 could over-scaffold role assignment, inflating apparent C1/C3 role security; mitigation: icons depict the referent category only (a cluster outline, a single bead), never quantities, and this scaffold is recorded as a presentation condition in the evidence map.
Read-aloud availability may under-detect the reading confound on ITEM-4 (highest text load) if she uses it, or leave the confound live if she does not; usage is logged per item either way.

The 'trick crate' framing on ITEM-4 tells her to be suspicious, which may cue 'different' without genuine referent discrimination; mitigation: the framing never mentions sameness, products, or swapping, and the numeric field (baskets in A = 2) provides a second, framing-independent evidence channel.

Identical seal feedback may cause second-guessing or repeated 'Needs another look' as a safe harbor; a not_sure rate across all four items is reported as an instrument-friction signal, not an ability signal.
Randomized-once option order on ITEM-3 controls position bias only weakly with n=1; the stored order permits post-hoc audit but not correction.

Touch mis-taps on a shared family device could seal an unintended entry; the disabled-until-complete stamp and clearable slots reduce but cannot eliminate this; anomalously low seal latency triggers the contract's inspection-threshold downgrade to evidence_ambiguous.
Warm aesthetic and finale could be read by adults as a mastery celebration; the completion line deliberately reports only crates handled, and the exported report contains no mastery language.
engagementPrediction: Prediction: given her documented appetite for difficult riddles and her persistence-with-scaffolding pattern, she will complete all four crates in a single sitting of roughly 4–8 minutes, will engage most visibly with the announced 'trick crate' (longer deliberation latency there than on ITEMs 1–3), and will use 'Needs another look' rather than random guessing if genuinely stuck — because the not_sure affordance maps onto her established hint-requesting behavior when blocked. Secondary prediction: the absence of correctness feedback will produce mild but tolerable friction (possibly one question aloud like 'was that right?'), absorbed by the inspector fiction rather than causing quitting. These are hypotheses derived from riddle-domain evidence only; the contract is explicit that none of it predicts multiplication competence, and this prediction claims nothing about her answers being correct.
falsifyingEvidence: Abandonment before ITEM-4 despite functioning interface falsifies the completion prediction and the claim that the inspector fiction sustains a no-feedback window for this child.

Repeated tapping of the sealed crate or the shelf, or verbal demands for correctness feedback that escalate to quitting, falsifies the claim that diegetic silence reads as world-logic rather than malfunction.

Guessing signatures — seal latencies below the inspection threshold on 3+ items, or zero use of 'Needs another look' combined with sub-threshold latencies — falsify the prediction that she stalls-and-asks rather than guesses, and trigger the contracted ambiguity downgrades.
Shorter deliberation on ITEM-4 than on ITEMs 1–3 falsifies the trick-crate engagement prediction.
Read-aloud used on every screen with long pre-response pauses falsifies the assumption that the one-sentence text load is negligible for her and elevates the reading confound on all items.

More than two 'Needs another look' responses falsifies the assumption that the affordance would be an occasional honesty valve rather than a dominant avoidance path, and marks the session as friction-dominated with mostly missing evidence.
Any observation of her answering to make the tower light 'faster' (e.g., stating she picked anything to move on) falsifies the claim that completion-based payoff does not pressure honesty.
measurementResponsibilities: Record, per item, the primary and secondary measurement keys exactly as contracted: c1_group_pair_correct, c1_roles_reversed, c1_reported_total_instead_of_pair, c1_not_sure_rate; c3_array_dimensions_correct, c3_roles_reversed, c3_reported_total_instead_of_dimensions, c3_off_by_one_count, c3_not_sure_rate; c2_equation_match_correct, c2_additive_distractor_selected, c2_duplicated_factor_distractor_selected, c2_product_only_recognition_flag, c2_not_sure_rate, c2_selection_latency_below_inspection_threshold; c4_referent_discrimination_correct, c4_same_selected_product_equality_confusion, c4_referent_count_correct, c4_ambiguity_flag_requires_followup, c4_not_sure_rate.

Capture latency keys (c1/c3 time_to_first_entry_ms, c2_time_to_selection_ms, c4_time_to_first_response_ms) via monotonic clock from stimulus-visible to first committed field interaction, and seal latency separately for guessing control.
Exclude from all scoring: reading time, keystroke/tap counts, pointer path, typing speed — logged only as friction context per the contract's exclusions.
Log accommodations and friction facts: read-aloud uses per element, slot clears, disabled-stamp taps, mute toggles, idle intervals over 60 s, ITEM-3 option order, device input type (touch/mouse).

Apply confound gating: downgrade sub-threshold correct responses to evidence_ambiguous; downgrade any item with flagged input/reading interference; always flag ITEM-4 'same' as evidence_ambiguous pending the disambiguation probe.
Run the cross-item consistency checks: dual role-reversal on ITEM-1+ITEM-2 flagged for ITEM-4 corroboration; correct ITEM-3 with incorrect ITEM-1/ITEM-2 flagged as probable product recognition.
Report completion factually: per-item terminal outcome from {correct, incorrect, not_sure, omitted, abandoned}; early exit records unreached items as missing evidence.

Produce only the contracted output: a per-construct evidence map (C1–C4) labeled supported-provisionally / contradicted / ambiguous / missing plus raised confound flags — no mastery, proficiency, grade-level, or preference declarations anywhere in the report; post-window hint usage, if any, logged in a separate record explicitly outside opening evidence.
